newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Proton to roll out its one millionth car.
newsitem.headline: Proton to roll out its one millionth car.

text.p: After 11 years of production, Malaysia's first national car maker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton) is set to roll out its one millionth unit on Monday.

The guest of honour at the ceremony at Proton's plant at Shah Alam -- an industrial area just outside capital city Kuala Lumpur --- will be Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, the mastermind behind the car project.
Mahathir is also expected to unveil a new 1.8-litre coupe model.
Though the road ahead may be slightly bumpy, analysts say the company is likely to motor along without too many breakdowns.

Already, Proton's acquisition of British sports car maker Lotus Group International Ltd in October for 51 million sterling has put it in good stead to develop its own engines and transmission systems.

"In the early years the emphasis was on production. They just wanted to produce as many cars as possible, and since it is a protected market, they did not worry too much about (developing) their own technology," said Choo Swee Kee, automobile analyst at equities research house Vickers Ballas in Kuala Lumpur.
When the first Proton rolled off the production lines in 1985 in a venture with Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp, the company was at the vanguard of Mahathir's industrialisation programme.
The government ensured the Proton was protected from competition from foreign car makers by slapping on a 300 percent import tarrif.
But international trade agreements will bring down import tariffs on foreign imported cars by 1998, forcing Proton to cut costs as one way to become more competitive.

"They are aiming to cut costs by 15 percent over the next five to six years. This year their costs will be cut by around three percent, but it gets harder to cut costs as you get nearer the bone," said Lim Kim See, automotive analyst at Omega Securities.
Another way to achieve greater economies of scale is by producing more cars. Proton plans to turn out 230,000 cars per annum by end of next year from 180,000 currently.
The company has also been aggressively marketing its cars overseas, pitting against more experienced Japanese and European car makers.
"They are behind on quality control, technology and cost efficiency," said Lim at Omega.
The Lotus acquisition was widely seen as a strategic move by Proton to obtain new car-making technology.
As Proton rolls out its one millionth car, analysts are confident that this is just another milestone on the road to becoming a world-class car maker. It already exports to some 30 countries.
"Whatever happens, the government will never allow Proton to die," said Choo at Vickers Ballas.
